title: Appellant v. EBRD, EBRDAT 2022-AT-01 Final Decision
text:
OFFICIAL USE
THE ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
OF THE
EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
Case No. 2022/AT/01
Appellant
vs.
European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
FINAL DECISION
by the Administrative Tribunal in plenum
26 January 2023
OFFICIAL USE

OFFICIAL USE
I. Introduction
1. With the present Appeal, the Appellant initially requested the Tribunal to recommend a
review of the provisions of the internal law of the European Bank for Reconstruction and
Development (“Bank”) on leave, in particular regarding the rules on parental leave.
2. In a prior appeal by this same Appellant on similar issues, the Tribunal had rendered a
decision on 26 August 2021. In that decision, the Tribunal rejected the Appellant’s request to direct
the Bank’s President to refer his case to the Administrative Review Committee (see Appellant v.
EBRD, EBRDAT 2021/AT/02).
II. Facts and procedural background
3. On 3 November 2020, the Appellant and his HR Business Partner discussed issues related
to his forthcoming fatherhood of twins by way of surrogacy, including his potential leave
entitlements. The Appellant had a number of queries to which his HR Business Partner indicated
she would look into and follow up with the respective clarifications.
4. In an extensive exchange of emails, a dispute arose about contents and application of the
Bank’s internal rules on parental leave in the Appellant’s specific circumstances. In an email of 4
January 2021, the Appellant was informed that he had “recourse under the Administrative Review
Process should [he] wish to pursue the matter further”. In another email of 17 February 2021, the
Appellant was advised that in case of disagreement he may seek “further review as set out in
Section IV, paragraph 6.4 of the ARP Directive.”
5. On 14 April 2021, the Appellant submitted such a request to the Bank’s President. On 5
May 2021, the President responded to the request informing the Appellant that she considered it
inadmissible. On 11 June 2021, the Appellant submitted an appeal to the Tribunal. In that appeal,
he requested to overturn the contested decision by the Bank’s President, and to direct her to refer
his case to the Administrative Review Committee.
6. In its decision of 26 August 2021 in case no. 2021/AT/02 (“Initial decision”), the Tribunal
clarified that the Appellant sought to call into question the Bank’s internal rules on parental leave
as such, rather than contesting an individual administrative decision in his specific case.
2
OFFICIAL USE

OFFICIAL USE
7. The present Appeal was lodged on 3 January 2022. The Appellant requests that “the Tribunal
recommend a review of the provisions contained in the Bank’s Leave Directive, Chapter IV
‘Parental Leave’, with view to avoiding and eliminating circumstances in which staff members are
subject to unjustified unequal treatment, specifically in cases of twin and multiple births”.
8. On 8 February 2022, the Bank filed a submission challenging the Tribunal’s jurisdiction,
arguing, on the one hand, that the dispute was res judicata, and, on the other hand, that the
application was time-barred. The Appellant submitted a reply on 28 February 2022.
9. The Tribunal rejected the challenge by decision of 22 March 2022 on both grounds. It held
that the initial decision had a different subject of dispute, and that there was no established time-
frame for filing the present (type of) appeal in the Bank’s internal rules.
10. Based on Rule 4.01 (g) of the Tribunal Appeals Procedures of the Tribunal, on 22 March
2022, the President of the Tribunal, through the Secretariat of the Tribunal, published on the
Bank’s intranet site a description of the present appeal relating to a Regulatory Decision as was
sufficient to enable amicus curiae briefs to be filed in accordance with Section 7.03 of the Directive
on the Appeals Process (DIR/2019/14). By 23 April 2022, four amicus curiae briefs had been
submitted.
11. On 26 April 2022, the Tribunal informed the Bank that no Response on the merits was
received within the time-limits set forth in Section IV, Article 4.04 of the Appeals Process
Directive. On 27 April 2022, the Bank requested to be provided with 20 working days to respond,
following receipt of the amicus curiae briefs. As there is no basis for such a request within the
Bank’s internal legal framework, the request was rejected on 6 May 2022.
12. On 7 May 2022, the Bank requested the Tribunal to hold an oral hearing. The Tribunal
granted the request and announced that the hearing would be held on 28 June 2022. It invited the
parties to inform the Secretariat of the Tribunal of the names and description of any witnesses and
experts whom that party would request to present oral evidence, indicating the points to which the
evidence was to refer.
13. On 31 May 2022, the Bank informed the Tribunal that the Bank, following internal
discussions, would undertake a review of its parental leave entitlements as reflected in the
3
OFFICIAL USE

OFFICIAL USE
Directive on Leave. Pursuant to this information, the Bank’s Human Resources Department
confirmed that it would recommend that the Board of Directors approve changes to the parental
leave provisions, which would have the effect of removing the differences in entitlements as they
related to circumstances of twin and/or multiple births. Relevant proposals and recommendations
for a decision by the Board of Directors would be made during the upcoming annual compensation
and benefits review.
14. Further, the Bank submitted that the aforementioned review by the Bank of its parental
leave entitlements for the Board of Directors’ approval/decision rendered the Appellant’s appeal
moot. The Bank confirmed it had already communicated the above to the Appellant and requested
the Tribunal to issue directions as necessary to account for the fact that the matter was now moot
and oral hearings were no longer required.
15. By interlocutory decision of 27 June 2022, the Tribunal suspended the proceedings and
requested the Bank to report to the Tribunal about the progress of changing its rules on parental
leave, including its results no later than 31 December 2022.
16. On 16 December 2022, the Bank reported that as part of the annual compensation and
benefits review, the Bank’s management submitted for approval by the Board of Directors a
proposal to provide the same amount of paid and unpaid leave for multiple births for a secondary
care giver for staff who take parental leave other than maternity leave (i.e. in cases of adoption and
surrogacy leave). In addition to the proposals on parental leave as it concerned multiple births in
cases of surrogacy and/or adoption leave, the Bank’s management also put forward a proposal to
extend the time for staff members who are secondary care givers to enable them to take their
parental leave within 12 months (instead of 22 weeks) after the birth of the child or from the date
that the child legally lives with a family in the case of adoption or surrogacy leave.
17. Further, the Bank reported that on 14 December 2022, the Board of Directors approved the
above-mentioned proposals as part of the annual compensation and benefits review, taking effect
as of 1 April 2023. Amendments to reflect the paid and unpaid leave for multiple births in cases
of surrogacy and adoption, as well as, extending the time from 22 weeks to 12 months for a
secondary care giver to take their parental leave would be incorporated into the Directive on Leave
and Procedure on Leave. All staff have been notified of the changes and the proposals are reflected
in the Bank’s intranet.
18. Against this background, the Bank requests the Tribunal to issue a final decision in this
matter considering that the contested regulatory decision in the Appellant’s appeal has been
4
OFFICIAL USE

OFFICIAL USE
addressed, as confirmed by the approved changes to the parental leave entitlement in relation to
multiple births.
19. The Appellant, in his comments of 16 January 2023, expresses his satisfaction that the
Bank acknowledged the merits of his appeal regarding its parental leave policies and the related
unequal treatment of parents of twins and multiple children through surrogacy, or by extension
adoption. He considers that “it was a very positive and welcome development that the Bank
proposed below changes before a final judgment by this Tribunal and that such changes were
approved by the Board of Directors at the end of 2022.”
III. The Tribunal’s evaluation
20. At the outset, the Tribunal takes note that the fundamental issues of the present dispute
have been addressed. The Tribunal notes with satisfaction the parties’ constructive approach,
resulting in an amendment of the Bank’s rules. As both parties expressed their satisfaction with
the solutions found, the Tribunal’s role is limited to an appropriate closure of the proceedings.
a) Applicable law
21. Pursuant to Section IV, paragraph 3.02 of the Appeals Process Directive, the Tribunal
“shall base its decisions on the provisions of the Staff Member’s contract of employment, the
internal law of the Bank and generally recognised principles of international administrative law”.
22. The scope of principles of international administrative law is not limited to matters of
substantive law. Rather, as the Tribunal has held in Case No. 2021/AT/02, para. 56 “it includes
principles of procedural law, e.g. the right to be heard (audiatur et altera pars)”. Also, the concept
of mootness is a principle of international administrative law, well established in the jurisprudence
of international administrative tribunals. For example, the United Nations Appeals Tribunal held
in a full bench decision:
“A judicial decision will be moot if any remedy issued would have no concrete effect
because it would be purely academic or events subsequent to joining issue have
deprived the proposed resolution of the dispute of practical significance; thus placing
the matter beyond the law, there no longer being an actual controversy between the
parties or the possibility of any ruling having an actual, real effect. The mootness
doctrine is a logical corollary to the court’s refusal to entertain suits for advisory or
speculative opinions. Just as a person may not bring a case about an already resolved
controversy (res judicata) so too he should not be able to continue a case when the
controversy is resolved during its pendency. The doctrine accordingly recognizes that
5
OFFICIAL USE

OFFICIAL USE
when a matter is resolved before judgment, judicial economy dictates that the courts
abjure decision” (see Kallon 2017 – UNAT – 742, para. 44).
b) Conclusions
23. The Tribunal reiterates that the Appellant limited his present appeal by requesting “the
Tribunal recommend a review of the provisions” contained in the Bank’s respective internal rules,
“with view to avoiding and eliminating circumstances in which staff members are subject to
unjustified unequal treatment, specifically in cases of twin and multiple births”.
24. By taking the decisions of 14 December 2022 (see above paragraph 16), the Bank has
addressed these concerns by reviewing and amending their provisions at stake. The Appellant
welcomes this development in his comments, without exception or reservation. The controversy
is resolved, and there is no room for further adjudication. Therefore, the appeal is moot.
IV. Request for anonymity
25. The Appellant requests to remain anonymous, and the Bank does not oppose this request.
The Tribunal grants this request, recalling that it is inherent to an appeal process that certain facts
and opinions become known, both inside and outside the Bank. This being said, it is the Tribunal’s
established approach to limit to the maximum extent possible, inter alia, the exposure of facts or
descriptions that may identify participants of the process.
V. Costs
26. Paragraph 8.06 (a) of the Appeals Directive provides:
If it upholds an Appeal, in whole or in part, the Tribunal may order that the respondent
reimburse the appellant for such reasonable expenses, including reasonable legal costs, the
appellant has incurred in presenting the Appeal. Exceptionally, the Tribunal may order that
the respondent pay all or some part of the appellant’s legal costs where the Appeal has not
succeeded.
6

OFFICIAL USE
27. As the Appellant was not represented by counsel and has not requested the Tribunal for
reimbursement, it is not necessary to enter into the question of whether the Respondent should pay
legal costs.
VI. Decision
27. The Appeal is moot, and this case is declared closed.
